maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   STUDY OF PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS OF FEDERAL REVENUES AND EXPENDITURES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   STUDY OF PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS OF FEDERAL REVENUES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister in connection with an article appearing in today's issue of Le Devoir. I would ask him whether the government has in its possession a study of the distribution of federal administration expenditures in the ten provinces and whether this document is, according to the report by Jean-Pierre Fournier, one of major importance in connection with Canada's economy and also the position of the province of Quebec.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   STUDY OF PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS OF FEDERAL REVENUES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will ask the Acting Minister of Finance to answer this question.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Acting Minister of Finance):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   STUDY OF PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS OF FEDERAL REVENUES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Department of Finance has been conducting a study of the allocation of federal revenues and expenditures among the ten provinces. This study is intended to provide material for answering questions on the subject asked by hon. members some months ago and referred to in the house the other day. Work has been going on in the department for months in anticipation of questions of this nature.
This subject was discussed at some length in the house on August 7 during the debate on the fiscal revision bill when the Minister of Finance indicated the nature of the work in progress and some of the difficulties being encountered. This study is only now being completed in the Department of Finance. The results are to be incorporated in replies to the questions asked hon. members; it has not yet been transmitted to the minister.
It will be evident that the assertions in the story in Le Devoir are untrue. The Minister of Finance was not given these completed figures three months ago, they have not been referred to the cabinet, and they have not been concealed.

Inquiries of the Ministry

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   STUDY OF PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS OF FEDERAL REVENUES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext: The hon. member for Ville-neuve.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   STUDY OF PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS OF FEDERAL REVENUES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question was already asked by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition.
My question was about the famous report which the government supposedly received more than three months ago.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   STUDY OF PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS OF FEDERAL REVENUES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to put a question to the Acting Minister of Finance to clarify the answer he gave the house a moment ago in connection with the study of the distribution of federal revenues.
Can he tell us whether or not the Minister of Finance has received a preliminary outline of the report to be submitted by his officials? If yes, can he say whether the minister has ordered a revision?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   STUDY OF PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS OF FEDERAL REVENUES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question is extremely complicated, and perhaps it would assist the house if I mentioned, for example, that one has to distribute sales tax collected at factories throughout all parts of the country. It would not be fair to say that all the sales tax collected at the factory in province A was paid by the consumers in province A; nor, for the same reason, would customs duties collected, for example, in the port of Montreal be properly attributed as revenues attributable to the province of Quebec, because those customs duties of course are paid by all Canadian consumers of those goods which pass through the port of Montreal. This is the nature of the problem; it is extremely complicated. The Minister of Finance has not seen any figures that have taken into account this redistribution of revenues collected at particular points.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   STUDY OF PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS OF FEDERAL REVENUES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext: My question was directed to learning whether a preliminary report had been submitted to the minister.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   STUDY OF PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS OF FEDERAL REVENUES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext: No preliminary report has been submitted which takes into account the factors that I have mentioned.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   STUDY OF PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS OF FEDERAL REVENUES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Was any preliminary report whatsoever submitted?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   STUDY OF PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS OF FEDERAL REVENUES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
I do not understand the nature of the question, Mr. Speaker. Of course, you can look at public records and find out how much customs duty is collected at various ports. That information is available to the Minister of Finance. He has never seen any


distribution of revenues amongst the ten provinces, as requested in the question asked in this house.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   STUDY OF PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS OF FEDERAL REVENUES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext: The hon. member for Lot-biniere.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   STUDY OF PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS OF FEDERAL REVENUES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Excuse me, Mr. Speaker, it is the second time that you have called my name. The question I wanted to put is the same as that put by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker).

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   STUDY OF PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS OF FEDERAL REVENUES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister.
Could he tell the house whether the government will have enough courage to publish those studies made on the distribution of the federal government's expenditures in the ten provinces, even if those figures were to show that the province of Quebec was the least favoured of all the provinces?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   STUDY OF PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS OF FEDERAL REVENUES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext: If the hon. member had listened and understood the answers given to this question he would have realized that this work is being done to secure information in reply to questions asked in the house and will automatically, of course, be made public. [Translation]

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   STUDY OF PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS OF FEDERAL REVENUES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a supplementary question.
I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he would agree to including two finance officials of the Quebec government among the officials of the federal government who are conducting this study, so as to eliminate the suspicions on the part of Quebeckers as to the objectiveness of certain federal officials?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS   STUDY OF PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS OF FEDERAL REVENUES AND EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Questions of this kind are answered on the responsibility of the government and with the advice and expert assistance of federal, not provincial, officials.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF ROYAL COMMISSION RECOMMENDATIONS BY DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE

speechtext: On the orders-of the day:

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF ROYAL COMMISSION RECOMMENDATIONS BY DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime

Minister, in view of the submissions which have been made to the respective provinces by the various colleges of physicians and surgeons, particularly the more recent submission to the government of Quebec, suggesting a health insurance plan which would have the effect of dividing Canada into haves and have nots, whether he will give the house the assurance that when the federal government meets with the provinces it intends to place before them a proposal which would adhere to the basic recommendations of the Hall commission, particularly the recommendation that health services under such a plan should be available to all Canadians irrespective of financial ability to pay and without any means test.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF ROYAL COMMISSION RECOMMENDATIONS BY DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend knows the recommendations of the Hall commission are being examined at the present time. The examination is concerned with a very important as well as a very complicated matter, and the Hall commission have made a very important series of recommendations. The examination will also be associated with consultation with the provinces in this matter. There is certainly no intention on the part of the government, in any action which I hope will be taken and put before the house, of making the kind of discrimination to which my hon. friend refers.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF REMITTANCE BY EMPLOYERS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF REMITTANCE BY EMPLOYERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of National Revenue. Is it the intention of the minister to make it

Inquiries of the Ministry compulsory for employers to remit weekly income taxes collected at the source on a weekly basis rather than on the present monthly basis, due and payable on the 15th of the following month?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF REMITTANCE BY EMPLOYERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member's question arises out of remarks I made recently in Montreal. At the present time the taxation division is studying the possibility of allowing employers to deposit the monthly remittances of taxes collected from employees in their local chartered banks to the credit of the federal government. At the time when employers in Canada make up their payrolls and deduct taxes from their employees, that money at that point is the property of the government of Canada. It is hoped that within a period of time after the practice to which I have referred has been put into operation, ultimately employers will enjoy the convenience of being able to deposit these collected taxes in their local chartered banks the same day they make up their payrolls. These taxes will be deposited to the credit of the government of Canada. It will be some time before this can be accomplished.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF REMITTANCE BY EMPLOYERS
speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Is the minister saying in his present statement that the taxes must be remitted weekly rather than monthly? Does he realize the great inconvenience which will be caused to small businessmen if this practice is instituted?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF REMITTANCE BY EMPLOYERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not say that. What I did say was that we are presently moving away from the practice of having monthly remittances made directly to the taxation division and toward a method of allowing the employers to deposit these taxes in their local chartered banks. I stated in my speech at Montreal that the ultimate step would be that the employers would deposit these taxes in their local banks at the same time as they write out their payroll cheques. The taxes collected belong to the government of Canada at the time they are collected. Under the present system there is some $100 million which remains in the hands of employers for a period of a month, and that money really belongs to the federal government.

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF REMITTANCE BY EMPLOYERS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I am sure from the minister's remarks that they will be made weekly. Am I correct in that assumption?

subtopic: PROPOSED CHANGE IN METHOD OF REMITTANCE BY EMPLOYERS
speechtext: No. It will depend on the payroll period, which may not be weekly. I should also like to point out to the hon. member that such a step is quite some disr tance away, because it will take us a good deal of time to get a system working whereby they can deposit monthly.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I notice in this report that the reason given for this increase by the companies concerned is an increase in the price of raw materials. As a very large proportion of these raw materials are derived from the developing countries of Africa and we have continuing reports of a decline in such prices, and complaints in this regard were again voiced by African delegates at the interparliamentary union conference in Copenhagen, is the minister prepared to investigate the situation and also investigate what appears to be considered evidence of a combination for price fixing among these large corporations?

speechtext:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration whether he is in a position to answer the question I put to him on October 1, which was whether he would allow the governments of the Yukon and Northwest Territories to participate as observers in the forthcoming federal-provincial conference on Indian affairs.
Inquiries of the Ministry [Translation]

speakeroldname: Hon. Rene Tremblay (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to answer the question asked by the hon. member and to inform the house that my colleague, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) and myself have decided to invite both commissioners of the Yukon and of the Northwest Territories, to attend that conference on Indians as observers. Also, some high officials of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources who have responsibility over education in both those territories will be invited to attend that conference.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Would the minister not agree that it would be equally appropriate to invite as observers some of the native Indian people themselves who have a vital interest in this question?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have already stated, that federal-provincial conference is at the level of ministers and officials of both governments. Its object is to discuss a program which will then be systematically submitted to all the Indians in the country.
I think this procedure is the best way to bring a solution to the problem, which is to co-ordinate policy. There should be an initial conference at government level and, then, discussions of various formulas with different Indian groups in order to have their suggestions concerning those programs.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Is the minister taking any steps to solicit the views and ideas of the Indian people on a national scale, inasmuch as their views should be placed before the participants in the conference at the time of their discussions?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
We thought it better first to hold a conference at the government level before inviting the comments of the Indians on those policies, because we want to be able to submit to the Indians a co-ordinated program implying participation, for various reasons, of the various administrative levels of the country.
We feel that the Indians will be more satisfied with a program which will have been

Inquiries of the Ministry discussed first from the administrative and financial viewpoints at the level of the various governments.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. I wonder if the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has consulted with his colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare to ascertain whether she has changed her mind about the fact that the Indians should be consulted prior to any of these discussions and prior to any decisions being made.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext: Before the minister answers that, may I ask a supplementary question. At the same time would he consider also the fact that while it is hoped the ministerial meeting to discuss Indian affairs will arrive at some conclusions, rather than presenting these conclusions to the Indians would it not be advisable to have Indian representatives present in order that they may be consulted at the time the decisions are being made?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, decisions will not be arrived at by that conference. At that meeting the federal and provincial governments will discuss the problems which might be raised by the extension of provincial services in the various provinces.
It is thought that a more systematic and efficient discussion might take place after the conference, if discussions were held during that conference they would involve both the relations of the governments with the Indians and those of the federal government with the provincial governments. It is felt that the interests of the Indians will be better served in this way.
This program in regard to the Indians includes no decisions whatsoever, but merely suggestions, and we shall be happy to make all the necessary changes in the program after we receive the recommendations and suggestions from the Indians.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister whether there has been any request from any Indian organization or band anywhere in this country to have the jurisdiction of the federal government over Indians sublet, transferred or assigned to the provinces. This is a very serious step and one that places the Indians in a position of subservience before the In-


dians have ever made any request for this. It looks like a very high handed practice.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say this. A distinction must necessarily be made between the provincial services which were extended in the field of education under the administration of the Leader of the Opposition as well as by other governments.
A distinction must be made between the availability of certain provincial services to the Indians and the transfer of jurisdiction.
As I said, it is not a matter of transferring federal jurisdiction to the provinces, and I know that all or most Indians in this country are opposed to the federal government's powers being transferred to any provincial government whatsoever. On the other hand, I am well aware that all our Indians are only too glad when they are given the same advantages as other provincial citizens where social security and education are concerned.
As for the way in which provincial services can be made available to Indians, we shall be glad to discuss the matter with the Indians so as to hear their opinions and their suggestions regarding these programs.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext: Then the minister has said that the Indians would be very satisfied to have certain jurisdiction-

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext: Not jurisdiction but the administration-

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I should like to get the
distinction, because if I cannot get it I feel sure the Indians are not likely to get it.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext: I am not too sure.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext: I do not know what the interruption was from the President of the Privy Council.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO TERRITORIAL PARTICIPATION IN CONFERENCE
speechtext: The minister says the Indians as a whole are desirous of having the advantage of the social services in the provinces. When did consultation with the Indians take place which leads him to make such a statement, which in my opinion has no justification?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all the officials of the Indian affairs branch are constantly in

touch with the Indian chiefs and the chairmen of the Indian councils, and the department has been aware for years of those needs, so much so that in the case of the province of Ontario, certain agreements have been reached with the provincial authorities in order to allow Indian children to attend Ontario schools. In fact, this trend has prevailed in Canada for many years.
But instead of reaching special agreements, what the government wants to do now is to establish an over-all program for the country, precisely so that what has been done for years in some provinces may be achieved within over-all programs, which will be to the greatest advantage of the Indians themselves.

speechtext: Is this general plan designed to provide an opportunity whereby the Eskimo problem in Labrador will be easily solved? Is this what is behind this plan?

speechtext: I wonder if I might direct a question to the acting house leader, further to the questions which have just been asked. replies to certain of the questions which have been asked the minister said decisions are made without consultation with the chiefs of

speechtext: One brief supplementary. Is the minister telling the house that the final solution to the Eskimo problem in Quebec will not be discussed at this conference?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved
speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
that the thirteenth report of the special committee on procedure, presented to the house on Wednesday, October 7, be now concurred in.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege and honour to move concurrence in the thirteenth report of the special committee on procedure and organization, and to do so on behalf of the committee. I trust hon. members have read this report, which was made part of Votes and Proceedings for Wednesday, October 7, but I think it would be desirable that a brief summary of what we are now proposing be given to the house and thus placed on Hansard at this time.
May I say at the outset that as with previous proposals which this committee has recommended to the house, we are suggesting that the ones we are now proposing be adopted for the remainder of the present session, unless otherwise ordered by the house.
We are making at this point, Mr. Speaker, proposals with respect to three phases of our procedure, and I shall now deal with them one at a time. In the first place we are proposing changes in standing order 26 (3). Standing order 26, as all hon. members know, is the one under which it is possible from time to time to seek to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance. So far as this standing order is concerned we are not proposing anything new, if one has in mind our present practices. However, there are two aspects of our present practice with

respect to standing order 26 which it might be said are not completely clear. What we are trying to do in this proposal is to tidy up standing order 26; we are trying to make these two points crystal clear.
The first point has to do with the right of members from the floor to speak to the question of debate before Your Honour rules whether there is such urgency. We propose that the right, which has now been accepted more or less in practice, be written into the rule itself. The sentence we propose to accomplish this is:
If Mr. Speaker questions the urgency of debate with respect to the proposed matter, he may invite members to speak on the question of such urgency.
The other point about standing order 26 concerning which there might be said to be some ambiguity is whether there is the right of appeal against Mr. Speaker's ruling in those cases where he rules that a motion is not of sufficient urgency to be allowed debate under the standing order. This matter has been debated a number of times and votes of the house have been taken. Those votes, as Your Honour and the previous Speaker know, have gone both ways. The majority of the votes and the more recent ones have been to the effect that there should not be an appeal. So we would write into the standing order words to the effect that, provided Mr. Speaker has listened to argument from the floor, any ruling that he then makes is not subject to appeal, and the sentence we propose to put into standing order 26, section (3) reads as follows:
Any ruling made by Mr. Speaker after listening to argument on the question of urgency shall not be subject to appeal, notwithstanding the provisions of standing order 12 (1).
Those then, Mr. Speaker, are the two matters concerned with standing order 26. As I say, we are tidying it up. We are writing into the rule what we have accepted in practice; and it is the general view of the committee, and I think the general view of members, that it would be a good idea to have this matter made definite. That is what we propose in the first of these three suggestions we now make.
I come now to the second of the proposals that Your Honour's committee presents to the house at this time, and it has to do with the resolution preceding what is called a money bill. As hon. members know, there has been discussion for a long time about the debate on a resolution preceding a money bill. Before 1955 there were two stages of debate prior to a money bill itself being presented;
Procedure Committee
there was debate on the motion for Mr. Speaker to leave the chair to go into committee of the whole on the resolution; then there was debate in committee of the whole on the resolution itself. In 1955 we amended the rule to eliminate the debate with Mr. Speaker in the chair, but we continued the debate in committee of the whole.
There has been an expression of opinion, which has been widely supported, that we might consider doing away with that stage of debate altogether. As a matter of fact there has been wide support for that abolition on the floor of this House of Commons. However, Mr. Speaker, there are procedural arguments for retaining at least a limited debate on a resolution preceding a money bill, and there is at least an element of doubt as to whether, under the constitution, we have the right to abolish the reference of such a resolution to a committee. I might say that very learned experts on parliamentary and constitutional procedures have said that doubt could be set aside, but if the doubt is there at all it seems to us that we should not fly in the face of it.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we are not recommending the abolition of the debate on a resolution preceding a money bill. We are in fact recommending that it be retained, but that the debate on such a resolution in the committee of the whole be limited to not more than one sitting day. We define a sitting day in our proposed standing order in what I think are explicit terms. We make it clear that if such a resolution preceding a money bill is the first item called under government orders on a Monday, Tuesday, Thursday or Friday, and if it continues to the end of any one of those days, that is a full sitting day, and at that point that debate is terminated. However, in order to make it possible for such an order to be called at some other time-as the second or third item on one of those days, or on a Wednesday-we provide that under any other circumstances than the first one I indicated, five hours of debate in committee of the whole on a resolution preceding a money bill shall be considered to be the equivalent of one sitting day.
Once we provide for a limit of that kind on a debate, obviously the question arises as to what happens if one, two or more people, who have unlimited time, take up a good portion of the day, and is that fair? We recommend that when we are in committee of the whole on a resolution preceding a money bill, notwithstanding the provisions of

Procedure Committee
other orders, all speakers shall be limited to 20 minutes. We make no change in the right to speak more than once, in other words no change in the right to ask questions and give answers, but we do limit each speaker to 20 minutes at any one time.
It will be seen that we are trying to get this debate back to its original character, namely an occasion when there can be inquiries and short statements about the financial provisions of the measure itself. Your committee, sir, is strongly in support of this proposition and believes it is a good one for the house to try out. Therefore we present it to the house in the name of Your Honour's committee at this time, and we hope it will commend itself to the house generally.
Sir, I come now to the third and last of the proposals contained in this thirteenth report, and this has to do with the consideration of clause 1 of bills when we are in the committee of the whole. There is a general feeling, certainly shared by the members of Your Honour's committee, that our opportunities for general debate are more numerous than they need be. We have the opportunity of a general debate on a resolution preceding a money bill. We have the opportunity of a general debate on second reading. Then immediately we get into committee of the whole it is possible to have another general debate on clause 1. Every bill also has somewhere- in clause 3 or 4, or perhaps in more than one- what might be called its main operative clause, and under that main operative clause it is possible to have wide general debate. We think that some of the length of time we spend, and some of the repetition in which we indulge, may be due to this arrangement. In most cases clause 1 of a bill provides only a short title. I might say that it is the practice in the parliament of the United Kingdom to have that short title at the end of the bill rather than as its first clause. We think, therefore, without changing the structure of bills at all, that there is a very simple answer to this situation.
We now have standing order No. 78 (1), which states that the title and the preamble are not considered until the rest of the clauses of the bill have been considered. We suggest that the same thing should apply to clause 1 of a bill, and that when we get into committee of the whole to consider a bill, clause 1 should not at that point be called if it contains only a short title. Of course if it is clause 1 of an amending bill and contains substance, or something other than the short

title, then this standing order will not apply. However, if clause 1 contains only a short title we suggest the committee move immediately to clause 2 and on through the clauses of the bill, and when all the other clauses have been dealt with, that clause 1 then be called.
May I point out, Mr. Speaker, that we are not eliminating the possibility of general debate in the committee of the whole, because there is in every bill a main operative clause. As I say, it is usually clause 3 or clause 4, in respect of which general discussion is possible. We are not even eliminating the possibility of general discussion on clause 1, because we are providing that it be called after the other clauses have been disposed of. But we believe that if at that point the bill has been thoroughly discussed, and possible amendments have been dealt with, the chances that members will want to discuss clause 1 at length are a bit on the slim side. We think, therefore, that technical though this change may seem-switching the discussion on clause 1 from the beginning to the end-it would have a time saving and useful effect.
Mr. Speaker, if the house will consider these last two proposals together-the second and third proposals of this report, limiting the debate on resolutions preceding money bills to one day, and transferring the consideration of clause 1 of bills to the end of the consideration by the committee of the whole-I think it will realize that we are making suggestions that do not in any way curtail or limit freedom of speech, and do not in any way interfere with the right of the fullest possible examination of measures that are brought before it, but that on the other hand they provide for sharper and crisper debate. We believe these proposals, which are being made in this house in the name of the special committee on procedure and organization, are good and worth-while proposals. We dare to believe that having tried them out the house will want to continue them in future sessions. At this moment we recommend that they be tried out from the time this report is adopted, as I trust it will be, until the end of the present session.
Therefore, on behalf of Your Honour's committee on procedure and organization, I commend this thirteenth report to the House of Commons for its endorsation.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr
Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has outlined, in more detail

than I shall attempt, the reasons behind the presentation of this report of Your Honour's committee to the house for its approval.
I should like to make one or two brief observations and a general comment. In respect of the question of appeal, it has been my view for some time, I think shared by other hon. members, that the whole question of appeals from Your Honour's rulings must receive consideration. There are many anomalies, not the least of which is the fact that basically the chairman of a standing committee has considerably more authority that Your Honour in that, as precedent now stands, there is no appeal from his ruling, nor can an appeal from his ruling be brought into the house for further consideration. This is one aspect which I think in due course will lead to a full report on this whole question.
However, in taking this step I assume we are conducting what might be termed a form of clinical research, because in presenting these amendments to the house for the duration of this session, the extent of which is now unknown, we will have an opportunity to see how they develop and work out in practice.
On the question of the discussion on the first clause in committee, there is no doubt in my mind that here there has been unnecessary and repetitious debate. I think this is a situation which might well be cured by the proposed amendment, and that even the most hardened offender in respect of the rule against repetition will be inclined to let the opportunity pass when he is confronted with the chance to repeat what he has already said after going through the clause by clause discussion in committee. If, on the other hand, something develops during the course of the clause by clause discussion which justifies him in making a further contribution, he has that opportunity.
The third item which did give us some concern was the question of the resolution stage on matters involving the expenditure of money, where a recommendation is made by the government to the house. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, there is a constitutional aspect which is of interest. There is, of course, another aspect which caused a great deal of concern and on which there was a considerable amount of discussion. In limiting the debate to one day we felt compelled, in spite of other standing orders of the house, to limit each member to 20 minutes. This trespasses, of course, on the traditional rights of the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition. As I say, this
Procedure Committee
matter did give us concern and evoked discussion and argument. I think I can safely say it was as a result of compromise that our recommendation was brought forward in this way. My view, Mr. Speaker, is that in due course I should like to see the complete abolition of the resolution stage, but there is grave doubt in that regard because of the possible constitutional cloud entailed in section 54 of the British North America Act.
There is also another aspect which hon. members will have in mind, namely that it is at the resolution stage that members have the opportunity to put forward alternatives to legislation which has not yet been presented. Once legislation has been introduced and comes up for second reading there are strong limitations on the opportunity of a member to make his views known as to possible alternatives. It would be my hope that at such time as we are able to agree to abolish the resolution stage we might also consider widening the powers of individual members to bring forward amendments, so they will not be bound and trammelled as they are today by the existing rules. It is quite notorious that the opportunity of a member in committee or elsewhere to bring forward substantive amendments is definitely limited, and the resolution stage on financial measures has provided some extension of that opportunity.
Finally, by way of general comment let me say that I am one of those who believe that the standing orders as they now are, with the addition of the precedents and decisions laid down over the years by Your Honour and your distinguished predecessors, are in sum total adequate to cover almost any contingency which may arise in the house. But that does not mean that from time to time members who feel they have a just cause to put forward do not override the rules. I am not inciting members to do this, but this is a situation which does develop because of the nature of the house, because of the type of men and women who are members of the house, and because of the issues which come before the house from time to time.
It has happened in the past that the rules have not always been adhered to, and it will happen again. I think it would be a sorry day for the house and the country if that did not happen, if we had a situation where a session would start and finish without someone, in pursuance of what he felt was a worthy and most desirable objective, going to lengths which the Chair might feel were in excess of the standing orders.

Procedure Committee
Having said that, it does not mean that we should not, in an effort to ensure that our procedures will be regular and that traffic will flow smoothly and adequately, make provision in minor ways for bridges, overpasses and stop lights so the traffic can be regulated and made to flow smoothly. In that sense, subject to what I have said, these are the types of amendments that the committee has offered to the house today.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member of the committee on procedure I take pleasure in joining with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Peace River in asking for concurrence of the house in these reports. I endorse the remarks that have already been made about them, and I hope and expect that all members of the house will do likewise.
Indeed, since one of the reasons for the recommendations is to remove some of the extraordinary repetition in debate that goes on in this chamber, I shall not violate the spirit of these recommendations by engaging now in any repetition of the excellent remarks that have already been made by the two hon. members 1 have just mentioned.
I would simply say that in my opinion these steps are very modest ones. Perhaps as a newcomer to the house one is more impatient to make somewhat sharper and more drastic reforms in the procedures of the house. These are modest steps but they are extremely important ones and will, I hope, lead to further reports in other areas in which there is an equal need for reform.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I should like to deal briefly with one of the concepts in the report, namely that there should not be an appeal from Your Honour's decision. May I say first that in essence I agree with this contention. However, without any disrespect to yourself and knowing that you will not take offence at what I am about to say, I would point out that the degree to which members accept the idea that there should not be appeals from your rulings will be influenced by the person who holds the office Your Honour now holds, and the circumstances under which he holds it.
For argument's sake, as long as we have a Speaker who at least at some time during his term of office engages in partisan activities-I refer now to elections-we are likely to have less than the desirable degree of respect for what is supposed to be the nonpartisan approach of the person who holds that office.
tMr. Baldwin.]
I think there would be greater acceptance of the principle of no appeals from Your Honour's rulings if Your Honour held the position permanently. If we had a situation in Canada, and I hope we will reach this stage, where the position of Speaker was a permanent one and the Speaker was not forced to engage in partisan activities at election time in order at least to be returned as a member of parliament, if not to hold the office of Speaker again, it would be much easier for us to accept the idea of no appeals from Your Honour's rulings.
We have advocated the concept that every constituency should be represented by a member who is able to speak on behalf of his constituents in the House of Commons and engage in the debates that take place. This is a privilege Your Honour does not now have. To this end we have suggested that members of parliament should elect the person to fill the position of Speaker and for that purpose we should declare the House of Commons to be a constituency so that Your Honour would in effect be our member of parliament. No constituency of Canada would thereby be deprived of a vocal member representing it by virtue of his attaining the office of Speaker. If we could get to this stage I think there would be a great desire on the part of members to accept the idea that Mr. Speaker's rulings should not be subject to appeal, regardless of the circumstances under which those rulings were issued.
It is fortunate, I think, that the proposed changes are to apply for a temporary period of time; that this is really to be a sort of testing period to see how the rules work in practice and whether the practice meets the theoretical concept the proposers had in the first instance. It has long been our contention that the debate at the resolution stage preceding money bills is rather superfluous. In effect we have had two second reading debates, one of them occurring at a time when we do not know the contents of the bill itself, except as they may be referred to in the resolution under consideration. In essence I endorse this idea that the debate at the resolution stage preceding money bills really creates a situation where superfluous debate can take place.
I would rather have seen the committee tackle this with a bit more firmness and attempt to eliminate debate at the resolution stage, rather than just confine it to one day and also restrict each speaker to 20 minutes. What I think is likely to occur is that we will

push the backbencher farther into the background during this debate at the resolution stage. It will, in effect, become a sort of leaders' day, even though there is a 20 minute time limit on speeches. Those who are leaders or who are in the forefront of their parties will have a greater opportunity to engage in this debate, and the backbencher will have a lesser opportunity than exists now to engage in the debate at that stage. As I have said, I would rather have seen the elimination of debate at this stage than to approach the matter in this way. The confinement of the debate will have a tendency to give less and less respect to the ideas and desires of the backbencher.
I have some reservations, too, about the effectiveness of the third proposal, that is consideration of clause 1 at the end of the bill. Even though this may not have been in accordance with the rules, even though the hope might not have been realized because of the exigencies of political activity in the house, we had looked upon the consideration of clause 1 of the bill as a time when, because we were in committee and it was possible to ask specific questions of the minister and get replies from him without closing the debate, we would have the opportunity to get some indication in a detailed way about the effect of the provisions of the bill which it is not possible to do during second reading. As you know, the second reading debate is more formalized, and when the minister speaks the second time he closes the debate and that is the end of consideration of the bill at that stage. Clause 1 did appear to provide an opportunity, especially for members of the opposition, to get more detailed information about the effect of the bill than was possible at second reading. This enables the opposition to make up their minds about the principle of the bill and its subsequent clauses, even though it might not be possible to refer in detail to any of the subsequent clauses.
I have some reservations, therefore, about the effect of the third proposal. However, my attitude about it is not put forward in a way that would lead to opposition to the proposal before us.
As I have said, these proposals are to be applied on an interim basis. There will be a testing period for these rules in the days ahead, just as there has been in the past in respect of changes in the rules. If these proposals, or some of them, become permanent we may be able to develop a set of rules that will permit the orderly dispatch of pub-20220-565
Procedure Committee
lie business and allow parliament to proceed in a more efficient way than has been the case in the past.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I only want to say a few words about this and to give general support to the recommendations of the committee. I urge concurrence in the motion by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
So far as the first proposal is concerned, that of tightening up the provisions of standing order No. 26, I think the present provisions make it almost a violation of the rules for Your Honour to ask for advice from members as to whether there is urgency of debate. I think it would be helpful to the Speaker at any time to invite some comments from various corners of the house before a decision is reached as to whether there is urgency of debate at the time. I believe, without being disrespectful at all, sir, it is quite impossible for Your Honour to be fully aware of current events in the country to the extent that you can independently, without some consideration, be called upon to make what may be called a snap judgment as to whether there is urgency of debate with regard to the matter raised. I believe it is a good thing to write into the standing order a formal provision enabling you to invite comment on the urgency of debate.
Then, of course, I agree that once you have made a decision there should not be any appeal from that decision. After all, after you had invited members to advise you on the urgency of debate in connection with the matter there certainly would have been some expression of opinion from members, and I feel we should have sufficient confidence in the Speaker to accept his decision after he has heard the advice of the members of the house.
The second proposal, namely restricting to some extent the debate that takes place on the resolution preceding a money bill, has been the subject of consideration for some time. I do not have the quotations in front of me, and even if I did I would not like to read all of them, but I think it is fair to say there have been expressions from spokesmen for all parties in this house that something should be done to restrict this particular debate. I go back to those opinions that were expressed when the committee on procedure and organization was set up. In the first place, I believe you will find the opinion expressed by all parties that something should

Procedure Committee
be done to either eliminate the debate on the resolution preceding a bill, or at least to tighten it up. I think the step taken here is probably the wisest one in the circumstances, because to do away entirely with the resolution stage proceedings in relation to money bills would raise constitutional problems involving the royal prerogative.
As far as proposal No. 3 is concerned, may I point out that we have witnessed in this house, during the last few months particularly, the development of what amounts to a further full scale debate on the first clause of a bill after it has been introduced in committee. This proposal would simply transfer discussion on the first clause to the end of the debate in committee, and then only if it contained the short title and nothing else. I therefore think there will probably be a disposition on the part of the house to pass this clause more quickly than in the past, since there would have been full discussion on all the other clauses of the bill before the discussion on the short title was reached.
In closing I should like to say that we in this party feel we should support these proposals on a trial basis. It is clearly stated in the recommendations that they be adopted on a trial basis for the remainder of this session, and that other arrangements can be made if they prove too restrictive or if further amendments can be brought in to enable the business of this house to be conducted more efficiently. We in this party are ready to support the suggestions for the balance of this session.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I fail to see the purpose or the necessity of extending the debate on the thirteenth report of the special committee on procedure and organization, presented today.
We, in this corner of the house, believe that any step to improve the Canadian parliamentary system, while respecting the rights and prerogatives of each member of parliament, should meet with the approval of the whole house.
Those are the few comments I wished to make. We are prepared to support any measure to improve parliamentary procedure.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I wish to say at once, as I have said on a number of occasions, that anything which can be done to improve the procedure of parliament without restricting the
[Mr. Olson.)
essential freedom and the traditional rights of parliament deserves support.
If you will allow me, sir-and I say this with diffidence with yourself in the chair- what has been done under your leadership has been the most unusual and effective action which has taken place during the quarter of a century, almost, that I have been a member of this house. You have convened a committee which has worked effectively, dispassionately and objectively. Too often he who occupies your ancient and honourable chair does not, in the nature of things, receive from members as a whole that expression of commendation which you have so richly earned. I want to say that I believe the committee has worked together in a way which does honour to its membership.
Parliament is subject to a great deal of criticism; it has been in recent years and months. But parliament, if its full function is understood, is carrying out the great responsibility which rests upon it. Indeed, it is the only institution which preserves and maintains freedom and which above everything else, assures that the humblest person in our land shall not be denied justice. We have had examples in the last few days of matters brought before the house concerning humble individuals. This is one of the major functions of parliament.
The hon. member for Skeena suggested that he would like to see established, or so I gathered from his remarks, a practice whereby a Speaker would become the member for a constituency to be designated for that purpose, and would not be subject to election as are other members of the house. That suggestion has been made in the past. It fails to give due emphasis to the fact that if such an arrangement were made the occupant of the Speaker's chair would not be the first commoner. The essence of being the first commoner is that among members who have been elected on a similar basis, whoever is chosen to be Speaker is, by tradition, the first commoner.
I have listened to the various arguments which have been advanced today respecting the recommendations, and I intend to refer briefly to three of these recommendations. First there is the proposal that Your Honour's ruling should not be subject to appeal on the question of whether the house should be adjourned to discuss a matter of urgent public importance. I think all of us are agreed that such a rule would simply implement the general practice, and that it is deserving of complete support.

As to the second proposal, I speak now not as one who occupies the position of Leader of the Opposition but as one who has been prime minister when I say I feel the house should give further consideration to the limitation of all members to 20 minutes under standing order 61A. The two officers of the house, the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, by reason of ancient right and modern application have certain duties and responsibilities. It is not that it will affect me; I am not speaking personally now, for I seldom speak at the resolution stage. But I think consideration might well be given to assuring the continuation of that principle, recognizing that the holders of those two positions have certain special responsibilities, and that the section in question might be amended, if the house is agreeable, so as not to apply to those for whom the rules have made provision for unlimited discussion.
With regard to the third recommendation, may I say I think it will be somewhat difficult to operate. I want to see this in operation. There will be no general discussion on clause 1. Hon. members would deal with the bill clause by clause yet, at the end, they would engage in a general discussion. However, it is something that is experimental and as such I give it my support, particularly in order to ascertain how it will work out. I have heard it argued in the past that this is a course that should be taken, and I welcome any changes that can be brought about without in any way undermining the traditional position of parliament. It is of that position that I am going to speak for a few minutes.
Everywhere there is criticism of parliament; it is becoming the general thing to do. The institution is subject to examination; our constitution is being carefully submitted to the searchlight of public discussion. The criticisms, as I summarize them, are these. Why does not parliament do more? Why does parliament only talk? Well, Mr. Speaker, parliament is a place where talk is necessary, and where talk preserved our freedom in two world wars. It is a place where talk brought about many of the changes that have been implemented following the general acceptance in the nation of views originally expressed in parliament, heterodox views which ultimately became the accepted.
The other day I looked back over the years and read how parliament was viewed in other generations. Some people feel they have really found out something, that parliament should be complained about and criticized. Certainly parliament's activities should be 20220-565J
Procedure Committee
examined carefully, but it is well to remember that there is really nothing new in the criticism. Someone has said that parliament pours out in characteristic words the characteristic heart of the nation. That is my concept of parliament. To carry it out, fair opportunities for discussion and decision must be provided. Criticism, however, which has no regard to the purpose, the history and the rights of parliament can be ill timed, if not dangerous.
I said a moment ago that I had read something of the criticisms of parliament in the past, and with the leave of the house I might place one or two quotations on the record. Samuel Pepys, on August 4, 1661 recorded that one of his acquaintances had told him:
How basely things have been carried on in parliament by the young men that did labour to-oppose all things that were moved by serious men. That they are the most profane swearing fellows that ever he heard in his life, which makes him think they will spoil all-
Charles Dickens, who sat in the press gallery in his day and generation for, I think,, several years summed up his views of parliament in these words:
The great dust heap of Westminster . . . laughing, coughing, oh'ing, groaning, a conglomeration of noise and confusion to be met within no other place in existence, not excepting Smithfield on a market day or a cockpit in all its glory.
I could quote Hazlitt and various political pundits. Robert Louis Stevenson summed it up in these words:
We all know what parliament is, and we are ashamed of it.
Another said:
Talk of mobs! See how few who have distinguished themselves in the House of Commons have ever done anything else.
Well, that is history; but it is living history today. What are the functions of the House of Commons? In order to criticize one must know what the functions are. The most important function is to control the finance of a country; to assure that money shall not be expended that has not been voted; that a full examination be made of all expenditures. The second is the expressive function; the expression of the minds of the people on all matters that come before parliament. The third is the informing function; and the fourth is to legislate.
In that order all political observers have placed the functions of parliament. You often hear parliament criticized for not governing. That is not the function or the duty or the responsibility of parliament. The responsibility is to deal with those matters that the

Procedure Committee
crown's executive brings before parliament, over and above, of course, the right of private members to introduce any measure that they deem fit. I mention this because it is so often said, "Why does not parliament get down to governing the nation?" That is not part of our duty. Ivor Jennings, the great authority, has said:
The function of parliament is not to govern but to criticize. Its criticism, too, is directed not so much toward the fundamental modification of government policy as to the education of public opinion.
Sir, you will never have an effective parliament by having a type of slot machine to turn out legislation. The quantity of legislation passed is not a measure of the effectiveness of parliament. Indeed, it was Gladstone himself who used these words in this regard, speaking to the House of Commons:
Your business is not to govern the country, but it is, if you see fit, to call to account those who govern it.
As I said a moment ago, there is widespread criticism largely based on the misconception that parliament does the nation's business and therefore anything that appears to take up time delays the business of parliament. As those of us who practice the art know, the business of the country is carried on not by parliament but by the administrative machinery of the government whether parliament is sitting or not. But parliament's responsibility and job is to give careful consideration to policy and the measures proposed to implement such policy. This it does by time-consuming efforts and processes. It scrutinizes; it questions; it explains; it criticizes. In other words, it talks.
Some say that parliament is not businesslike, that it should be run on the lines of a business. Again such a concept assigns to parliament a role it does not have, the administration of the country's business. What parliament must do, however, is to oversee and compel by criticism effective and efficient practices in the departments. If it were not for the fact that parliament talks, many of the legislative enactments brought before the House of Commons would lead to endless amendments as weaknesses were discovered. We must always, in the limitation of debate in parliament, recognize this fact; that any new policy or legislation should not receive a less gruelling testing than any piece of machinery or manufactured material receives before it is prepared and readied for sale. If it were not for parliament making a long and complete examination, disastrous measures, the weaknesses of which would not otherwise

be exposed, would be passed if there was too great a limitation on discussion.
Let me also say, Mr. Speaker, in speaking of parliament, that I often see parliament criticized because its debates are too prolix; there is bitterness, and strong arguments are advanced along this line of thought. Those who make that criticism do not know parliament. They should read the debates in the British House of Commons. Let me recall one example, where Aneurin Bevan followed upon Winston Churchill, as he then was, and said "I wish, Mr. Speaker, immediately to puncture this bladder of falsehood by the poniard of truth". They are words almost Churchillian in their import and power. Immediately someone wanted to have Mr. Bevan called to order, but he said "I was quoting". As Your Honour knows, if an hon. member makes a quotation and applies it to anyone, no withdrawal can be demanded. For the next week or so there was a great deal of discussion in the letter press of the United Kingdom as to who was the author of these powerful words. Some said it was Shakespeare; although they could not find the exact quotation they knew it was there. Others said it was Beaumont and Fletcher. Others claimed it was some other Elizabethan dramatist. Finally, two weeks later, when no withdrawal could be asked on a question of privilege, when he was making a further speech Bevan was asked whom he was quoting and he replied "I was quoting myself." That is the parliament of the United Kingdom. As you said the other day, Mr. Speaker, let us not be thin-skinned, and that is so. Maintaining decorum does not mean the restriction of strong and definite language. Yet one of the criticisms of parliament has been that arguments have been too strong, too direct. I would ask those who hold that view to read the debates of 1920 and 1921, 1925 and 1926 and 1932 and 1933. By comparison this parliament is represented by featherdusting members. I am not asking hon. members to go back to the days of Macdonald and Laurier and Borden, but I do say that much of the criticism of parliament, to the effect that when arguments are advanced members are wrangling, does not pay tribute to the critic for his knowledge of parliament, its antecedents or indeed its recent past.
I am glad to see that this committee brought forth these recommendations unanimously. I believe that recommendations can only be effective if they are made unanimously; indeed, they ought not be brought in by your committee, sir, without unanimity.

To do otherwise would be to defeat the very object we have in mind, which is by agreement to bring about those changes which are necessary to meet changing conditions without in any way diminishing the mandate of parliament and its traditional power. The setting up of a Speaker's permanent committee on procedure with the continuation of its deliberations from year to year would, I am sure, receive general support from all members.
There is one other matter in connection with parliament. No matter what we do on the floor of parliament here the press of our country has a tremendous responsibility to make available to the people the fullest and most unbiased of information. We have been blessed throughout the years with a very good press gallery. However, what I say is this, that we will never have strong, free institutions without the presentation by the fourth estate of the fullest information on parliament. I know, as do all of us, that what is unusual, spectacular, weird or unorthodox is always newsworthy. Although I have said this before, I should like to see other newspapers across the country following the example of one or two which are already providing each day a summary of what has taken place. I am not speaking for myself now, sir, but for the backbench member who works hard, prepares a speech, gives a great deal of study to what he has presented, and finds that he is not even mentioned as having been an also ran.
I do not suggest that full summaries should be given, but the kind of reference that the London Times makes from day to day has a tremendous influence upon the quality of debate and also provides incentives to members in the preparation of their speeches.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, as well as all hon. members, have particular

The changes that are recommended today represent steps forward. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, much has been done by committees under your leadership, Mr. Speaker.
