speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minisfer):
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about the report of the committee, which I am happy to support, and to make a comment along the lines of the very interesting observations made this morning by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) in discussing this report. He pointed out, and I think we are all very conscious of this, that the recommendations of this report deal with the procedures of parliament at a time when our parliamentary institutions are under a great deal of examination and much criticism. As the right hon. gentleman reminded us, it is, however, useful to keep contemporary criticism in perspective. Parliamentary institutions from the very beginning of parliament have always been subjected to the criticism of those who are impatient, quite often understandably impatient, to get things done even at times at the expense of careful consideration and discussion.
We often read, Mr. Speaker, about the apparent indifference of members of the House of Commons to the proceedings of the house as evidenced by their lack of attendance, and on that point I realize that at the moment I am not speaking to what might be called a large and enthusiastic audience.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Those who are interested are here.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
But those who make this criticism do not always make allowances for the other things that members of parliament have to do, and do not always realize that

Procedure Committee there has always been this kind of criticism of parliament and parliamentarians. The classic story in this regard, of course, is the passing by the British parliament almost 100 years ago of the British North America Act, the act that founded our confederation, which was passed in a practically empty House of Commons at Westminster after a short and perfunctory debate, we are told that once the British' North America Act was disposed of the county members especially trooped in and filled the house because the next item of business was a dog tax bill.
It is not very long ago that I read in the newspaper a very important speech indeed on foreign affairs by the chairman of the senate foreign relations committee in Washington. It was one of the most significant speeches in recent times but it was delivered to a senate consisting of three senators. So the audience perhaps does not always determine the importance of the observations that are made. I hope not.
We were also reminded by the Leader of the Opposition this morning that our manners in the House of Commons are criticized whereas in reality we are models of decorum compared with what used to go on in the house 50, 75 and 100 years ago. Indeed the right hon. gentleman this morning referred to us, including himself, as featherdusters in debate. Perhaps I am, but he is not.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: You are not either.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It is true, of course, that we are under examination and criticism. All institutions, especially all popular institutions based on discussion, are under criticism today. That criticism and examination are the more significant and the more noticeable because of the development of media of communication that did not exist 50 years ago and which can bring our defects, even more than our virtues, to the attention of a very large audience within a few minutes of the delivery of our speeches. Indeed, sometimes they can do it before we have even made the speeches. This has had some bearing on the position of parliament and parliamentary institutions.
I should like to echo what the right hon. gentleman said this morning about the importance not only of responsible speech and action in the house but the importance of responsible reporting of what is said and done here. I say that, not in criticism at all but in recognition of the importance of those who serve the public so well by reporting what goes on in parliament. It must be very

tempting indeed to report our deliberations in terms of the more exciting phases of those deliberations, and excitement can always be created by conflict.
Conflict is, of course, its own publicity agent. Sometimes the careful, thoughtful, quiet speech with constructive proposals does not get the same amount of attention. However, while it is useful and I think well to keep things in perspective, I do not myself get as much comfort perhaps as I should out of comparisons. In the old days, and the old days do not mean more than 25 or 50 years ago, it did not matter as much as it does now whether or not we were inefficient in our procedures. The day when we could secure immunity from the consequences of our own inefficiency, in the light of the importance of what we are doing, has gone.
It was not very long ago when the government of the day was perplexed, not with the problem of getting things done but with the problem of finding enough things to do tc keep parliament going for three months. In that kind of situation it did not matter very much if debate on a bill went on from Monday until Friday or the next Friday because the government was often hunting for something to take its place. Those days have gone by and whatever may have been the case in the past we cannot any longer afford the luxury of inefficiency of any kind in the conduct of our proceedings. Nor can we any longer assume that in the case of parliamentarians repetition means reputation. I hope whatever we do, and this hope was expressed in eloquent terms this morning by the righl hon. gentleman, to change our rules and oui proceedings-and I am glad we are making progress in that regard-there will always be preserved as the very foundation of our parliamentary institutions the right of full anc free discussion. I think it goes without saying that that principle would be subscribed tc by every member of the house. Perhaps we would not have the same unanimity witl regard to the application of the principle tc a particular case as to what constitutes ful! discussion.
The right of discussion is of importance but of equal importance is the right o: decision after a full and free discussion. The abuse of the right of decision can be equally damaging to parliamentary institutions as the abuse of the right of discussion. We have tc reconcile these two things. This is a problen which is much more complicated and difficul now than it has been in the past.

The setting up of this committee under your chairmanship, Mr. Speaker, to look into our procedure was I think one of the most constructive things that has been done by parliament for many years. I have been very proud, as the leader of the government, to be associated with the initiation of this work. I should like to pay my tribute to you, Mr. Speaker, as chairman of the committee and echo the other tributes that have been paid to you by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition; also to the members who have worked so well and so effectively on the committee and its subcommittees. The appointment of the committee and the work that has been done by the committee and its subcommittees -and perhaps I could make a special reference to the hon. member who is chairman of a subcommittee whose report we are considering-is a reflection of the desire of members to speed up and make more effective our parliamentary deliberations.
I agree, Mr. Speaker, that this is the right way to proceed in reforming, reinvigorating and strengthening our parliamentary procedures, that is, by a decision of an all party committee and by a decision which, whenever possible, is unanimous. This is the right way to proceed. However, although it is the right way to proceed, I hope we will not lose sight of the fact it is important that progress be made and that the committees be not unduly handicapped or delayed by the necessity, on every single occasion, of reaching a unanimous decision. It may well be that when the committee and subcommittee-this could have been their experience already-approach some vitally important aspect of this question there may be difficulty in getting unanimity. I hope that the desire for unanimity will not prevent progress.
I support and approve of the recommendations in this report. I could have wished, and I suppose members of the committee could have wished, that some of the recommendations could have gone farther. The fact that they did not go farther is not, I believe, an indication that the committee will not continue its work and bring in even more important recommendations in the future. I believe myself, and I have been saying this in the house when in opposition and in government, that the most important change we could make now, and I hope it will be made before long by a unanimous report of the committee, is the introduction of a procedure by which time could be allocated on all the proposals that are introduced in this house for discussion and decision. The beginning
Procedure Committee
of this process of time allocation is to be found I believe in the recommendations before us today. I hope this will be only the beginning. So far as we are concerned on the government side, we support the allocation of time by agreement on legislative proposals so that we will know, in the government and in the opposition, in an approximate way at least when parliament is beginning how much time will be required for the legislation which is on the order paper. The committee report does not go so far as that, Mr. Speaker, but it does make some very useful proposals.
In dealing with the resolution stage, as has been pointed out by previous speakers, while not doing away with that stage, the proceedings are limited in time. I am one of those who thought perhaps we could do away completely with the resolution stage of money bills. It is a hangover, if I may use that expression, from the long distant past, going back to Stuart times when the resolution stage of money bills was the protection of the commons against the crown. We do not have to worry about that now. While the resolution stage is retained, it is certainly limited and it is vastly improved by the recommendations made. It is suggested that the time allowed for consideration of the resolution stage be now reduced to one sitting day, deemed to be a total of five hours. I think, Mr. Speaker, this is all to the good. It does represent an agreement on time allocation in certain circumstances.
The second portion of this recommendation restricts all speakers at the resolution stage to 20 minutes or less. The Leader of the Opposition made some observations on this recommendation this morning which I confess I found rather impressive. He pointed out that this would put the Prime Minister and Leader of the Opposition in exactly the same position as any other member of the house with regard to time limitation. There are, I believe, four or five standing orders which do except the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition from the time limitation applied to other members of the house. It is not easy to talk about this when one is personally affected by them, but these exceptions are based, I think, on a sound principle, namely that the leader of a government in introducing legislation is in a special position of responsibility and may require, and usually does require, more time than a private member for the purpose of explaining the bill to the House of Commons on behalf of the government. And I think the Leader of the Opposition, occupying another position recog-

Procedure Committee
nized by the house itself, should be given the same privilege when replying to the Prime Minister. I think a case could be made for maintaining this extension even in respect of a debate on the resolution stage which is limited to one day.
There has been no motion made on this matter and it would not, I believe, be in order to move an amendment even if that were desirable, and I do not intend to do so any more than did the Leader of the Opposition. I certainly would not wish to take any step which would result in the reference back to the committee of this report -a report with which I am in agreement. I should like, however, to make the point that these recommendations apply for the present session of parliament only, and I suggest that when the committee meets after they have been in effect, should the house adopt them, its members should look again at this particular subclause of the recommendations to see whether the considerations advanced by the Leader of the Opposition and myself do not warrant further consideration of this matter.
I think it is a very useful change indeed to put to the end the debate on the first clause of a bill in the committee stage, rather than have it at the beginning of the proceedings. I hope this will work out satisfactorily and I believe it will, for reasons which were mentioned in the discussion this morning.
I am in hearty agreement with the proposal that your decision, Mr. Speaker, with regard to motions to adjourn the house should be final and not debatable. The proposal in this respect reads:
Any ruling made by Mr. Speaker after listening to arguments on the question of urgency shall not be subject to appeal.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN THIRTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It
is not my intention to detain the house at any length but I hope hon. members will permit me to congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, and the members of your committee on this report and on the other reports which are now before us.
I think these reports fully vindicate the action which was taken by the house in setting up this committee. I agree with the statement which has just been made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) that this is the most desirable procedure to adopt in changing our parliamentary procedure when it needs to be changed. I do not mean by this that all changes must wait on complete unanimity. There may be occasions when changes will have to be made in the procedures of the house without waiting for every last party

and every last member in the house to be in complete agreement. But if it is possible to get unanimity in making changes, then that is the most desirable course to follow. I imagine all members of the house feel pleased, as I do, that the reports now before us have the concurrence of all the members of these respective committees.
It is the essence of a parliamentary system that we never get changes exactly as we want them if we wish to get a consensus from all parts of the house. But I would imagine that these changes which are proposed in this thirteenth report-and I speak for the party with which I am associated-constitute a very substantial improvement. The first proposal with reference to the change in standing order 26 is identical with the eighth proposal which I made a short time ago when putting forward ten proposals for a parliamentary reform program. I think it has two great advantages; it will set out clearly the right of a member to outline the urgency of debate, as well as clearly establishing the practice we have been following in saying there is no right of appeal against a Speaker's ruling on this question.
With reference to the resolution stage of so-called money bills, we in this party would prefer to eliminate it altogether. I know that in most of the provincial legislatures this stage has in fact been eliminated. They have met the problem of reference to the crown by having a provision attached to the first reading of money bills; before first reading is called the minister concerned simply reads a statement signed by the representative of the crown to the effect that the bill has been submitted to His Honour the Lieutenant Governor who recommends it for the consideration of the legislature. In this way the reference to the crown is continued. This practice also prevents a private member introducing a money bill because, of course, he cannot obtain the necessary written statement. It seems to me there should be no constitutional difficulty about eliminating the resolution stage as a prelude to money bills. But the proposal which is made here goes a very long way. At least it is a substantial improvement and I think ought to be given a fair trial.
Both the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) have made reference to the 20 minute limitation. Normally I would agree that both these officers of the house ought to have extra time.
I think, however, there are some arguments for not doing so in this case. The first is that if the debate is going to be limited to the reduced sitting hours on a Wednesday or 20220-566
Procedure Committee
Friday, or limited to a day on Monday, Tuesday or Thursday, if the two leaders of the house have unlimited time, between them they could take up three fifths of the time. This has been known to happen-not in the case of the present incumbents necessarily, but it has been known to happen in days gone by when we had three hour and four hour speeches. Therefore I think there has to be some limitation.
But I think the second reason is more important. The primary function of the resolution stage, if we are to have one, is for short statements on the principle and particularly to ask questions; because that is why the resolution is in committee stage, rather than going through second reading, which was eliminated by the house in 1955. It seems to me that for short statements and questions and answers the 20 minute rule is sufficient. The committee will of course watch the effect this has as we proceed with it, but I would hope they will recommend maintaining it unless some very good reasons come to the fore as to why it should not be continued.
The third recommendation with reference to the debate on the first clause of a bill in committee of the whole is I think an eminently sensible proposal. I sat for some years in a provincial legislature where for many, many years-in fact, for several decades-the short title of the bill was always the last clause called. It was found that by the time members had gone through all the clauses in the bill many of the questions which they might have asked on clause 1 had already been answered, and this procedure reduced the debate very considerably. I think this is a wise proposal which has been made by the committee and is certainly worthy of a trial run by the house.
I want to say just a word or two about the general idea of parliamentary reform. Both the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) have said quite properly that parliament is under some criticism. I think we will deceive ourselves if we keep saying that this criticism is because the public is ill informed or because people today live in a complex age and are in too much of a hurry. If parliament is under criticism we ought to ask ourselves whether a good deal of this criticism is not fully justified. The Leader of the Opposition said that one criticism is that parliament only talks. I think, more realistically, the criticism is that members of parliament too often talk

Procedure Committee
just for the sake of talking. I think people expect us to talk, but I believe they feel there is little value in constant repetition day after day when members are repeating what was said the day before and are repeating it again at subsequent stages of the passage of the legislation.
The objection is not to the fact that parliament is a place for debate so much as the feeling on the part of the general public that tedious repetition is out of place in a parliament where the business of the country is of paramount importance. The task which faces Your Honour's committee, and ultimately the house, is to try to find that fine balance between complete freedom of expression for all the elected representatives and at the same time have due regard for the efficient dispatch of business so as to provide adequate time for the examination of estimates and expenditures, which is one of the functions of parliament.
It was said this morning that the amount of legislation passed is not the criterion of parliament. That may be true; but what is the criterion of parliament? It is a reflection on the efficiency of parliament if some legislation takes a long time to pass through the house because of unnecessary and tedious repetition and at the same time other legislation of equal or greater importance is left to the dying days of the session and is either not passed at all or is rushed through with little consideration. We have all had the experience in days gone by of hundreds of millions of dollars of estimates being rushed through the house in the dying days of the session. This has never been an example of good business procedure to give to the people of Canada. That is why we in this party have long felt-and we hope the committee will consider this- that we should follow the example of the parliament at Westminster of establishing an annual timetable and plan the work of parliament, so that we do not dawdle for weeks or even months on some matters which may be of importance, and neglect other matters which are of equal importance.
We hope the committee will look into the role of committees of the house. We hope they will study the question of private members' bills. It is a frustrating experience for private members to prepare bills and find it is impossible to obtain a decision of the house and they are simply talked out. We hope Your Honour's committee will look at the question of the allocation of time for debate. We think this would do a great deal to speed up the business and to distribute

time as between different pieces of legislation and different functions of the house.
I must say in closing, Mr. Speaker, that in the final analysis I am sure we all recognize that no matter what the rules and the procedures of the house may be, the efficient conduct of business in parliament depends upon self-discipline on the part of members, co-operation among all the parties in the house, and mutual confidence and trust as between the leaders and the members of the different parties. This is something of course that cannot be written into the rules; it can only be generated by the good will of the members themselves. Mr. Speaker, I want to give my support and the support of this party to the work of the committee and offer them our congratulations. We trust that the support and the favourable comments they have received today will encourage them to carry on their work with continued success.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to become involved in any contentious discussion, but when we hear the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) agreeing so quickly, we know there is some comfort in the House of Commons, and that the hon. member has seen the light for the first time since his election.
The amendment I eventually intend to propose is related to part 2 of the committee's report dealing with debates in the committee of the whole house on resolutions preceding bills involving the expenditure of public money. Paragraph 2 of the proposed new standing order 61A reads:
Notwithstanding the provisions of any other standing order, no member shall speak for more than 20 minutes during the time when a resolution preceding a bill involving the expenditure of public money is under consideration in the committee of the whole house.
It has always been accepted that, by our rules, extra time will be given to the prime minister, a minister of the government, or a government member to explain a measure carefully to the House of Commons. Extra time has always been given to the leader of the official opposition and the leaders of other parties during the debate on resolutions. I feel the proposed new paragraph of this standing order will curtail the prime minister, ministers of the government, the leader of the opposition, leaders of other parties, or government members explaining resolutions.
As the Leader of the Opposition pointed out, it is not the function of the House of Commons to govern, but rather it is the function of the executive or administration to govern. In other words, the government governs, whereas the House of Commons ap-

proves or disapproves of policy or legislation, and scrutinizes very carefully the proposed expenditures which are made from time to time.
As has been suggested by the leader of the official opposition, the leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Thompson) and the Prime Minister, I think extra time should be granted to the prime minister, ministers of the government or government members to explain resolutions presented to the house, particularly when they relate to the expenditure of public money. I always think the leader of the official opposition and the leaders of other opposition parties should be given extra time to reply in respect of those resolutions. To do otherwise I think would unnecessarily curtail the debate.
Mr. Speaker, standing order No. 31 reads:
When Mr. Speaker is in the chair, no member, except the prime minister and the leader of the opposition, or a minister moving a government order and the member speaking in reply immediately after such minister, or a member making a motion of "no confidence" in the government and a minister replying thereto, shall speak for more than 40 minutes at a time in any debate.
You will note there that an exception is made in respect of the prime minister, the leader of the opposition and ministers moving motions. I suggest that exception should be extended and applied in reference to paragraph 2 of the new proposed standing order 61A.
There have been times when the business of this parliament has been delayed, and perhaps on occasion these delays have been caused by the official opposition, whether it be Liberal or Conservative. I am sure the members of the splinter parties will not mind my stating that I was in this house when there was only one splinter party consisting of eight members. It is hardly necessary for me to point out that we now have five parties in this House of Commons. In spite of the fact that the leader of the New Democratic party states that his party represents two million voters, the more parties we have in the House of Commons the more delays we experience. It might well be that the New Democratic party would not represent even one million voters if the public was made aware of that fact.
Unless we are willing to get into the position in which France found itself, I think some improvements have to be made in the rules. Some consideration must be given to a reform of our debates in parliament. When
Procedure Committee
the parliamentary system was first devised we only had a two party system.

I will finish my remarks and then answer any questions. My time is somewhat limited and I do not want to delay proceedings at this stage. I want to refer to another portion of the address by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
The title "prime minister" has found its way into some of our federal legislation, but it is interesting to note that even today those rather important statutes, important to the individuals concerned at any rate, which provide for the salaries paid to the leaders of the government and the opposition designate the one as the Queen's first minister but the other as leader of the opposition.
First of all, the point I am making is that the leader of the official opposition is a part of the government, and I repeat that as the parliamentary system got under way and matured through crystallizing traditions and customs, it really matured around a two party system. I am not saying that we should have only a two party system because I believe in democracy and at the present time the Canadian people are prepared to elect five parties. We do not know what they will do in the future. I know that these remarks will receive a sensitive reaction. We are just as sensitive when we are criticized and the government is just as sensitive when it is criticized. However, I would think it is only fair to parliament and the Canadian people to point out that if there were eight parties in the house instead of five as we have now there would be more delay. Therefore I am happy to see that the rules have been streamlined in that regard.
Let us see what the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has had to say about the role of the opposition. On January 27, 1959, he spoke at a luncheon meeting of the Canadian club of Ottawa and in his speech he quoted from very good authorities. At that time he was leader of the opposition and he quoted with approval a statement made by the then prime minister, now Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). I said that the leader of the : official opposition speaks for the official opposition. He or someone designated by him or his party speaks for the official opposition and they have a very important function in the government of Canada. The present Prime Minister quoted with approval what the then prime minister had said on one occasion, and I would point out that similar words were . used by another leader of our party, Arthur Meighen, to whom the present Prime Minister has referred with complete approval. This is - the quotation the present Prime Minister used in his speech:

"If parliament is to be preserved as a living institution, His Majesty's loyal opposition must fearlessly perform its functions. When it properly discharges them the preservation of our freedom is assured. The reading of history proves that freedom always dies when criticism ends. It upholds and maintains the rights of minorities against majorities. It must be vigilant against oppression and unjust invasions by the cabinet of the rights of the people. It should supervise all expenditures and prevent over expenditure by exposing to the light of public opinion wasteful expenditures or worse. It finds fault; it suggests amendments; it asks questions and elicits information; it arouses, educates and molds public opinion by voice and vote. It must scrutinize every action by the government."
In doing so it prevents the short cuts through democratic procedures that governments like to take. The present Prime Minister pointed out in a real punch line the all important function of the official opposition when he said that the absence of a strong opposition means a one party state, and a one party state means an all powerful cabinet. I would point out that there are 96 members of the official opposition and I think anyone will agree that at times it is a pretty strong opposition. Let us see who else the Prime Minister quoted with approval in his address to the Canadian club. He referred to what the late Right Hon. R. B. Bennett had said when speaking in the house on March 23, 1932:
"Oppositions are essential and necessary in the development of a democratic state. They serve a great and useful purpose. To the extent that criticism is frank and thorough, to that extent they do a great service to the country."
Then the Prime Minister referred to Benjamin Disraeli and with some sense of humour apologized to his audience for quoting from Conservative sources but said he had done so because he had found that on this matter these sources were good. He quoted these words of Disraeli:
No government can be long secure without a formidable opposition.
Then the Prime Minister went on to say:
I must confess, however, that it is not my conception of the role of the opposition to be formidable so that the government can be secure.
Then he quoted these words of Edmund Burke:
He that wrestles with us strengthens our nerves and sharpens our skill. Our antagonist is our helper.
The point I want to make is that the official opposition has a very important role wher it comes to government. Let us see what tha' role really is. Let us summarize it. First o: all, it has been said earlier today by the Leader of the Opposition and others tha

its role is to scrutinize expenditures, to approve or disapprove government policy, to approve or disapprove legislation and to do so with care because if it is not scrutinized carefully it will be subject to many amendments. Because of the training of the people in the official opposition they should always be in a position at any time to be able to take over the government. I think anyone will agree with that. That would seem to be a function of the official opposition.
I want to go further. I want to say that I was impressed with what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre had to say in his speech. I do not want to delay the house but I would ask every member to read what that hon. member said on March 21, 1957. His address can be found in the library, bound in a red book. I have a photostatic copy of it. Hon. members should read it, and it is not nonsense as the hon. member for Port Arthur has said.
The official opposition has an important function because they must be more responsible that any other opposition party. The statements made by the official opposition must be made with a greater sense of responsibility because tomorrow they may move over to the other side of the house. They are in the position to do so.
You will recall the first parliament of 1962, Mr. Speaker, when the Liberals were even stronger in numbers in opposition than we are now. It was only a short time until they took office as the government. This is what has happened throughout the course of history since confederation.
The function of the official opposition has been made clear by distinguished writers and parliamentarians, but members of the official opposition must always remember their responsibility in any statements they make. If they offer criticisms or make suggestions they must be in a position to implement their suggestions and to change the things they have criticized when they take over the government. If they fail to do that then they are not equipped with the responsibility to govern.
I want to repeat that I had hoped to hear the leaders say they would approve an amendment or suggestion that the time allotted to a prime minister or other government member presenting a resolution of this kind should be unlimited, just as in other cases, and the same courtesy should be extended to a leader of the official opposition. If the New Democratic party approves that,
Procedure Committee
if the leader of the Social Credit party approves that and if through the Prime Minister the government and the Liberal members approve it, it seems to me we could simplify the procedure today. If we are all unanimous in that regard this slight change can be made and then the report can be approved expeditiously. But one can never be sure and, as I said at the beginning, I have taken the responsibility for my party of making this suggestion because it was approved by the party.
I should like therefore to present this amendment. If in the course of presenting the amendment everybody approves of it, then it can be incorporated in the report and it would not be necessary to send the report back to the committee. I believe the suggestions that have been made for the changes in the rules, other than this slight amendment I have, are good and will expedite the business of this house and will add dignity to it.
I too congratulate the members of the committee. I was a member of the committee for a short time and I congratulate the members of the committee on the job they have done. I know how much work must have gone into this report. I want to congratulate you, too, Mr. Speaker.
I wish to move now, seconded by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler):
That the motion be amended by striking out all the words after "be'' and substituting therefor:
"not now concurred in, but be referred back to the special committee on procedure and organization with instructions to amend subsection (2) of the proposed standing order 61A as referred to in paragraph 5 of the said report by striking out all the words following the word "member" in line 2 of the said subsection (2) and substituting the following:

In that connection I point out that we are now in the 166th day of the sittings of this session and the committee report in which concurrence has now been moved recommends that we try these changes until the end of this session.
The difficulty with the amendment, as I see it, is this: It undoubtedly deals with something that was omitted from the committee's report, a point on which the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister both expressed reservations. I was interested to note that their remarks, if I heard them correctly, concerned the right of extra time for the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister because of the special obligations or duties they have to this house.
[Mr. Speaker.)
The motion as moved is in somewhat wider language in that it gives that same extended period for speaking to any minister moving a resolution. In any event, I do not wish to argue the merits of the point in detail now. The point obviously has some substance in it. We are in this situation; the committee has done some rather excellent work. I think all the speakers who have preceded me have spoken well of the work done by the committee. The committee has brought in a report and these amended rules would be in effect to the end of this session. The amendment would send this report back to the committee with an instruction of this house when the house has not, as is obvious from the discussion, given the amount of detailed study that should be given the proposed amendment. I suggest a better course-because there is no way of amending a proposed amendment to a standing order being enacted by way of moving concurrence in a committee report even with unanimous consent, as was suggested by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams). The house can only give unanimous consent for itself and cannot give unanimous consent on behalf of the committee. It is just not possible for the course suggested by the hon. member for Bow River to be followed. I ask the hon. member to consider withdrawing his amendment and adopting the motion for concurrence in this report which all speakers so far have favoured rather clearly. Then, we could leave it to the members of the committee, who are here in the house, to consider right away the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition, the Prime Minister and the mover of the motion, and they can bring forth whatever further reports they think appropriate.
In this way, when that new motion for concurrence comes up for decision in this house we will not be in a position where this whole day's debate will have been wasted and the whole subject can be debated again. We will have concurred in the report today as recommended by the committee and I think it will be reasonable to expect that the committee-though, of course, I cannot speak for the committee and I do not presume to do so-would consider the matter and in due course bring us something further on this point. I expect too, that its considerations would be limited to this point only, so the debate which would later take place would be restricted in its scope.
In the light of these remarks I wonder whether the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) would consider taking an-

other course. Feeling as I do about the work of the committee I am unwilling to repudiate its work, in effect, by sending the whole report back. At the same time I fully appreciate the remarks which were made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) on this particular point and I am in accord with them. This is a dilemma in which, I suspect, many members of the house find themselves. I hope the hon. member will consider what I have said and see fit to withdraw his amendment and permit concurrence in the report of the committee.

Mr. Speaker, a few words only to underline the inconsistency of those who clamour for the improvement of the Canadian parliamentary procedure and the elimination, when possible, of useless debates.
The committee, which is representative of all the parties in this house, suggests that the debate on the resolution preceding a money bill be limited to five hours. Everybody admits that one day's debate, at the resolution stage, is sufficient, for since we do not have the bill then, we do not know how it will be drafted.
Besides, when the bill is introduced, we still have an opportunity, at the second reading stage, to discuss the principle of the bill; moreover, when section 1 of the bill is called we are allowed by the rules and procedures to debate the purpose of the bill. At that time the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) may both speak for as many minutes or as many hours as they see fit.
Mr. Speaker, the members of the committee were congratulated for having submitted to the house a report so well documented, so well prepared and so consistent. But an amendment is being moved to the effect that the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition might speak as long as they wish, which means that if the Leader of the Opposition speaks for two hours and a half and the head of the government does the same, this totals five hours and there is no time left for the other members who wish to

participate in the debate. Hon. members would no longer be able to discuss the object of the resolution, since the debate would be limited to five hours.
Mr. Speaker, I sincerely feel the amendment should be re-examined by the committee either next week or the week after. In my opinion, the proposal made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is reasonable and acceptable.
If we did not take part in the discussion before this, it is because we wanted to allow passage of the motion to shorten useless debate in the house. That is the attitude of our party and I will not delay the house any further now.

I do not think that is a great deal of assistance, Mr. Speaker, although I appreciate the try. Bill No. C-56 has not been presented to the house before. The reason for bringing it in really relates to representations I have received from certain people who are interested in the mutual fund and the investment fund business. These people made the point to me that there is a practice that is more than a tendency for mutual funds to take advice from firms that in a sense are captive to their own, and to take this advice, instead of at a negotiated fee, at a percentage of the volume of business handled. As a consequence, if it is a quarter of 1 per cent, it sometimes has gone as high as 1J per cent, and then the amount of money that is made by the investment firm is extremely high.
Given a well managed fund and a good return, I do not suppose any investor is going to complain about this. But the representations brought to my attention were by people who pointed out the identity, if you want, between the senior officers of the investment firms and the senior officers of the investment analysis and advisory people. It is rather

obvious, particularly if you have read the book "The Grim Truth About Mutual Funds" by Ralph Lee Smith, that this practice has caused serious concern in the securities and exchange commission of the United States. This identity of interest is a means of giving an extra reward and profit in the operations to officers of mutual funds organizations. The effect of this amendment to the Criminal Code is contained in the bill as follows:
-when his undertaking so entered into or continued may or does conflict in interest with an obligation of whatever nature by him owed in whatever capacity to any other person-
And so on. That means that if you have an investment analysis organization which is a subsidiary or, in effect, a captive in control of a fund or trust company, the compensation or benefits entered into by the people who are advising the organization are under a very definite control by the Criminal Code. The explanatory notes state:
The principle of this bill has been applied to, and presently binds, members of this house and the Senate-by each house in its orders and rules and by parliament as a law of Canada.
That is inserted to emphasize the fact this principle does apply.
On this particular question of advice which brings financial gain, I realize how difficult and complex a problem one gets into when you look at all the various kinds of organizations which in a sense are advisory and at the same time may be considered captive. One of the reasons I felt an amendment to the Criminal Code would be worth while-and obviously it is not possible to come at this through any securities and exchange regulation-is that it would be there as something which could be invoked and brought up when something of this kind became a very evident scandal, rather than something which would be in application all the time where there are these kind of financial relationships.
I know it would be difficult in the case of certain lawyers and legal firms. For example, I can think of several in my own area to which this would apply. There is nothing wrong in what they are doing, but in effect several lawyers are partners in construction firms which do a fair amount of building and construction work. This is a sideline for them in a separate company. At the same time they are the legal advisers to the firm. I had not any intention in introducing this particular amendment to create any difficulties in an organization of that kind; I was thinking more specifically of the kind of public company operating in the trust and investment field

whereby, as a means of providing an extra profit or some extra kudos to some of the senior executives, this advisory agency is set up and is given a percentage of all that which is invested by the major company, which would ensure a very tidy income which, in terms of the amount of time and skill put into it, just does not really seem justified. In essence it is a fictitious value which is created by this type of advice. I do not know how widespread is this practice in Canada but I do know from two different mutual organizations to whose representatives I have talked that the situation does exist in Canada.
There is very little more I want to say about this bill other than that I should like to see some interest in this question of mutual funds and investment funds, the way they receive advice and that advice is paid for. I happen to have some kind of certificate-I do not know that it actually represents shares-which I got a few years ago from a mutual fund in connection with a plan which sends your children to university. I have no complaint of the purchase which I made or the whole framework of the operation, but I do feel that if a particular company has an expanding order of business, as this one has, and if their investment advisers are dealing essentially with the same market, no matter how much money the firm has to invest it does not seem to me that a straight percentage of income from that amount of investment and investment growth is really fair. It seems to me that this is sloughing off some of the profits which should go to the actual investors in the fund.
Despite the humour and embarrassment of the situation, Mr. Speaker, I regret that in a sense I have belittled my own bill as a result of the rather over-glamorous or overgimmicky name attached to the title of "the King's evil". This shows how much confusion at least one member of parliament can get into and I apologize to the house and to my colleagues for the mistake I made. I also express my appreciation to the "boy from the valley", if I may put it that way, for drawing this mistake to the attention of myself and the house.

For the Janusary of Mammon who has everything-*

I want to speak on the nature of the bill itself. Again, I am not trained in the law; I am simply a person who tries to read and understand the English language, and I have difficulty understanding this bill. Clause 1 reads in part as follows:
Every one who, for compensation or benefit of any kind whatsoever, enters into or continues a party to any contract, agreement, or relationship, whereby he undertakes, in whatever capacity, to sell or furnish to any person any investment, managerial, financial, legal, engineering, purchasing, marketing, auditing, statistical, advertising, publicity, tax, research, or other service, information, or data, when his undertaking so entered into or continued may or does conflict in interest with an obligation of whatever nature-
This is a very sweeping indictment. Conflict is of the nature of things in our society. This is certainly so in our political life. The problem, Mr. Speaker, is not the existence of conflict. I think that the problem with which the hon. member is attempting to cope is the situation in which there is a lack of full and complete knowledge on the part of everyone concerned of the nature of the conflict, where there is inadequate disclosure of the situation in which a person may put himself, having more than one obligation which is not apparent to the parties with whom that particular person is dealing, where there is a situation in which ties that may exist are not public knowledge or not knowledge or information within the possession of the affected parties. I think that is the kind of situation where the injury lies.
In my own life, for example, I have engaged a solicitor to act for me in the purchase of a house. I knew at the time that this same solicitor had also searched the title for the vendor, had done the initial' work on the property and was familiar with the title. The individual was well known to me. He is a man in whose competence I have to this day absolutely unquestioning faith and to whom I would trust my own personal possessions and reputation without any question whatsoever. That man was in a position of conflict as I understand the drafting of this clause, and he would be subject to a criminal penalty. If I have improperly understood the clause I should like some hon. member to tell me in what respect I have misunderstood it.
It seems to me that the hon. member has cast much too broad a net for the purpose

he has in mind. Legislation should be specific. Legislation should deal with specific evils in a very specific way. An attempt to do too much, to use language that is too inclusive, to prescribe penalties in situations where they would not be enforced, does not result in the kind of legislation that according to my understanding of the law should be enacted in this house.
I come back to my initial point. What is the purpose of a private members' bill? I think the hon. member has a most laudable purpose. He wants to call attention to certain situations where conflict exists, where there is harm done, and I think the best way in which the house can deal with this problem is to debate it at some considerable length. I would be very much surprised if the time of one hour would be sufficient to permit a subject as broad and as important as this to be disposed of by the house.

It is a fact that there are parasites in the world of finance, people who extort money from the public through all sorts of fraudulent ways and means.
For instance, not too long ago there were mine promoters in northern Ontario; indeed, we had some too in northwestern Quebec. Those people, who were not truly mine promoters, stole large amounts of money from average citizens and workers who had some savings.
When fantastic ore deposits were discovered in the Timmins area recently, swindlers rushed to areas located 40 and 50 miles away from Timmins, and formed mining companies with respect to properties which had absolutely nothing in common with the site on which the ore was found. Federal charters as well as provincial charters were the object of speculation. In any case, people were swindled out of their funds. This is plain robbery, no less, of the small investor.
Such practices have taken place and still take place in our country in many fields, not only in the sale of mining stock. I have just referred to a recent instance, but thousands upon thousands of small investors are losing their savings in this way. Among them are workers, miners, labourers, or farmers who sold their cattle and their property in order to buy stock in such mining companies on the strength of some tip they claim to have got about this or that mining stock. They had been told that in a matter of months, they would get three or five times the money they had put in.
Today these people are grievously concerned; they are in a sad predicament. Why? Precisely on account of those sharpers paid by stock market operators to extort the workers' money.

The same thing happened in the Timmins area. It is still being done. No provincial or federal government ever steps in to put a stop to those financial intrigues designed to take unfair advantage of plain folk.

I wish to direct the attention of the house to one or two aspects of this bill and I think I can do so in less than two or three minutes.
If it is the intention of the hon. member by this proposal to amend the Criminal Code to strike against certain specific ills, then to that extent, to the extent of his explanation, I have sympathy with his motives though not necessarily with the methods he is attempting to use. An examination of the wording used in this bill indicates, as one hon. member has already said, that far too wide a loop is being cast compared with the result which it is intended to achieve.
I think we must understand the distinction between the civil and the criminal law. Most actions which are the subject of prohibition by the Criminal Code can be the subject of civil proceedings. From time to time under common law where there has been a conflict of interest reflected in a breach of trust by one acting in a fiduciary capacity there has been, and is, a right of action in civil law. But when we come to take from the civil law certain acts and brand them as being so evil in their nature that they should be characterized as criminal offences liable to the penalties of criminal as well as of civil law, I think we must be precise and accurate in our definitions. We must recall that a crown prosecutor called upon to seek a conviction under a section of the Crimial Code has the onus of proving his case beyond any reasonable doubt, and I think it would be most difficult for a crown prosecutor faced with the necessity of asking a jury to return a verdict of guilty to succeed, having regard to the wording which is now used in this measure.
The complexity of the world today makes for so many forms of inter-relationship between people, social, moral and legal that the wording used by the hon. member would, I fear, place a great burden upon the law officers of the crown if it were allowed to become part of the criminal law.

It matters little to us on this side of the house whether the hon. member hangs himself on the Judas tree or whether he does away with himself by an overdose of the King's evil. Whichever it is, we would be quite satisfied. I was disturbed by the admonitions of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hahn), that if this bill were passed the hon. member for Port Arthur would have to give up one or other of his vocations. I, personally, enjoy reading his column. There have been some very prominent people mentioned in that column. I had the unfortunate experience of using his column as part of my election literature in a recent ill-fated campaign in which I participated, and I was assured by my supporters that the use of the hon. member's column was the very thing which finished once and for all my chances of success in that campaign, and I never read it thereafter. Nevertheless, I personally miss his column. The unfortunate thing would be that if the hon. member were to lose his seat I know he would never gain a place in the press gallery, from his standing with that honourable body of gentlemen, and we would therefore be obliged to do without his column. So I sincerely hope this bill will not pass and that the hon. member will be able to continue bringing a little ray of sunshine into many lives in many places.
I would add one or two words with regard to the general tenor of the bill. I agree with the hon. member for Carleton, that its provisions are too sweeping having regard to the ends which are sought. To this extent it is typical of socialist solutions. With one fell swoop they would cure all the ills of the world. Here they are trying to cure a broad area of ills by one paragraph in one bill. I do agree that in this day and time there is a great need for the protection of the individual citizen in many areas against those in corporate positions of power whether in government or in business. There is talk of legislation to protect consumers. If members wish to talk about an individual citizen in this area as a consumer, it might be good terminology. I think we have done a very

subtopic: REFERENCE TO INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION ON RED RIVER POLLUTION

speechtext:
October 1, 1964.
Dear Mr. Chance,
I have the honour to advise you that the governments of the United States and Canada have been informed that the waters crossing the international boundary in the Red river are polluted by sewage and industrial wastes. Having in mind the provisions of article IV of the boundary waters treaty signed January 11, 1909, that boundary waters and waters flowing across the boundary shall not be polluted on either side to the injury of health or property on the other side, the two governments have agreed upon a joint reference of the matter to the international joint commission, pursuant to the provisions of article IX of said treaty. The commission requested to inquire into and report to the two governments upon the following questions:
(1)	Are the waters referred to in the preceding paragraph being polluted on either side of the international boundary to an extent which is causing, or likely to cause, injury to health or property on the other side of the boundary?
(2)	If the foregoing question is answered in the affirmative, to what extent, by what causes, and in what localities is such pollution taking place?
(3)	If the commission should find that pollution of the character just referred to is taking place, what remedial measures would, in its judgment, be most practicable from the economic, sanitary and other points of view and what would be the probable cost thereof?
For the purpose of assisting the commission in making the investigation and recommendations provided for in this reference, the two governments will, upon request, make available to the commission the services of engineers and other specially qualified personnel of their governmental agencies, and such information and technical data as may have been acquired by such agencies or as may be acquired by them during the course of the investigation.
It would be appreciated if the commission would submit its report and recommendations to the two governments as soon as practicable.
Yours sincerely,
Paul Martin
Mr. D. G. Chance, Secretary,
Canadian Section,
International Joint Commission,
303 Fuller Building,
75 Albert Street,
Ottawa.
Tuesday, October 13, 1984
